results.summary: ESC syncope guideline. An implantable loop recorder is indicated (Class I) early in the evaluation of recurrent syncope of uncertain origin with a high likelihood of recurrence within the battery life, and in high-risk patients in whom a comprehensive evaluation did not find a cause. External loop recorders should be considered early when the interval between symptoms is 4 weeks or less (Class IIa). A loop recorder may be considered when epilepsy was suspected but treatment has proven ineffective (Class IIb).

results.summary: ESC syncope guideline. Myoclonic jerks in syncope are usually brief, arrhythmic and begin after the loss of consciousness, and recovery of orientation is fast; prolonged post-event confusion favours an epileptic seizure. Cardiac pacing is indicated (Class I) in patients with syncope and documented symptomatic intermittent or paroxysmal intrinsic second- or third-degree AV block.

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a 41-year-old woman with a 12-year label of refractory focal epilepsy presents after her fifth convulsive episode in two months on two antiseizure drugs. The ECG shows only PR 192 ms, the echo and cardiac MRI are normal, and telemetry and a 28-day event monitor record no episode. The implantable loop recorder records paroxysmal complete AV block with asystole up to 27 s during three witnessed episodes, which calls for permanent pacing, withdrawal of the antiseizure drugs starting with lamotrigine, and genetic evaluation for familial conduction disease.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Three red herrings (the epilepsy label, an 'aura', a non-diagnostic event monitor); the diagnosis needs a loop recorder after non-diagnostic short monitoring; the management adds the lamotrigine conduction warning and the family history of conduction disease.

Patient 2 (41-year-old female with 12-year refractory epilepsy label, complete heart block on ILR) provided the demographic and clinical seed. patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Elena Vargas is a 41-year-old Hispanic female elementary school teacher with a 12-year diagnosis of 'refractory focal epilepsy' who presents to the emergency department via ambulance after her fifth episode of sudden loss of consciousness with convulsive activity in the past two months. Today's event occurred at approximately 11:45 AM while she was sitting at her desk grading papers. Her husband, who happened to be visiting the school, witnessed the episode in its entirety. He reports she made no sound before the event and was not moving or agitated. She abruptly went pale and collapsed out of her chair onto the floor. She had bilateral arm and leg jerking for approximately 15-20 seconds. She was completely unresponsive during the event. She regained consciousness within 25-30 seconds with no post-ictal confusion, asking only 'Did it happen again?' She was in her usual mental state within approximately one minute. EMS arrival approximately 10 minutes later found her alert, oriented, and requesting that her husband call a substitute teacher. She reported no preceding headache, visual changes, epigastric aura, deja vu, or palpitations before this or prior episodes. She denies any chest pain, dyspnea, or leg swelling. She does note that prior episodes have occurred in a variety of positions and settings — sitting, standing, and once during sleep — without consistent positional or emotional triggers. She recalls one 'warning' before a prior episode — a brief sensation of 'ringing in the left ear' lasting two to three seconds, which has been attributed by her neurologist to an epileptic aura. Her current antiepileptic regimen includes levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily, both at therapeutic levels on last check six months ago. She has previously failed valproate (hepatotoxicity), carbamazepine (hyponatremia), and phenytoin (intolerance). Her neurologist considered her 'pharmacologically refractory' and had discussed possible epilepsy surgery evaluation. A routine EEG obtained six months ago was reported as normal. A 24-hour ambulatory EEG obtained three months ago was also normal and captured no events. Brain MRI three years ago was reported as normal. Her husband mentions that her father has a pacemaker for 'heart problems' and asks whether the heart could be involved. The emergency physician has ordered a 12-lead ECG and called cardiology for consultation.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue laceration from the current event. A well-healed scar is visible on the occiput from a prior fall. Husband, who witnessed today's episode, reports the patient suddenly went pale and glassy-eyed, then dropped straight to the floor without warning, followed by rhythmic jerking of both arms and legs lasting approximately 15-20 seconds. She was unresponsive for approximately 25 seconds total, then woke up asking 'Did it happen again?' with no confusion beyond that initial question. He noted she had no prodromal aura, no cry, and appeared 'like someone had hit a switch.' Cardiac examination: regular rhythm at 62 bpm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Jugular venous pressure normal. No peripheral edema.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive 3mm to 2mm. No papilledema on fundoscopy. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact, no nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact in all three divisions. Masseter symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with voluntary activation; no droop. CN VIII: Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag intact. CN XI: SCM and trapezius 5/5. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait, normal base and stride. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. Appropriate affect, mildly anxious. Attention intact — serial 7s without error. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. No post-ictal confusion at time of evaluation, approximately 50 minutes after the most recent episode. No dysarthria or paraphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. No spasticity, rigidity, or fasciculations. Strength 5/5 in all major muscle groups bilaterally. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception intact in all four extremities. No sensory level or dermatomal loss.
